INTJ.desc: You map out the big picture and push long-term goals through on your own. You value competence and efficiency and tend to judge by logic rather than feelings.

INTP.desc: You need to understand how things work. You love taking ideas apart and prefer original solutions over set routines.

ENTJ.desc: Once a goal is set, you rally people and resources and execute fast. Decisive and efficiency-minded, you can sometimes miss how others feel.

ENTP.desc: You hunt for new possibilities and sharpen ideas through debate. Quick and articulate, you're energized by new challenges, not repetition.
weaknesses: Love of debate can be misread

INFJ.desc: You read people well and want work that matters. Quiet but firm in your beliefs, you rarely bend on values you've chosen.

INFP.desc: You have clear personal values and deep empathy. You enjoy creative expression and want authentic relationships and work.

ENFJ.desc: You see potential in people and help them grow together. Great at reading the room and connecting people, you sometimes neglect yourself.

ENFP.desc: You dive into new people and ideas with curiosity and enthusiasm. You brighten the room and spot possibilities, but finishing what you start can be hard.

ISTJ.desc: You get the job done responsibly. You judge by facts and experience and take procedures and promises seriously.

ISFJ.desc: You quietly look after the people around you and fulfill your duties. You notice small changes but tend to put your own needs last.

ESTJ.desc: You set up order and systems so things run reliably. You have clear standards and strong drive, but can seem strict to people who work differently.

ESFJ.desc: You value harmony and look after everyone. Sociable and dependable, you're often the center of the group but care a lot about others' opinions.

ISTP.desc: You solve problems hands-on by figuring out how things work. Calm under pressure and efficient, you tend to put off emotional talk and long-term plans.

ISFP.desc: You enjoy the present moment and treasure your own sense of style. Kind and modest, you tend to quietly step back from conflict.

ESTP.desc: You act first and shine in the moment. You read situations fast and turn crises into chances, but sometimes miss long-term consequences.

ESFP.short: Born entertainer who lights up the room
ESFP.desc: You create fun wherever people gather. You live in the moment and express feelings openly, but planning ahead is a challenge.

mbtiTest.title: MBTI Personality Test
mbtiTest.description: 48 questions, about 5 minutes. A free, unofficial 16-type personality test with 5-point answers
mbtiTest.shareText: My MBTI is {type} ({nickname})! Take the test →
mbtiTest.disclaimer: An unofficial test for fun and self-reflection. MBTI® is a registered trademark of The Myers-Briggs Company; this is not the official MBTI assessment.

scoring.title: How scoring works
items: Each of the four axes has 12 statements, 6 of them reverse-worded, so a habit of agreeing with everything (acquiescence bias) does not push your result to one side.
Each answer becomes -2 to +2 points, summed per axis and shown as the percentage toward the first letter (E/S/T/J). The four axes are scored independently.
The side above 50% sets the letter; an exact 50% tie goes to I/N/F/P.
If neither side reaches 60%, the axis is marked "Borderline" — both preferences are close and the letter may change on a retake.

what.title: What is MBTI?
items: MBTI (Myers-Briggs Type Indicator) is a personality type classification tool
It classifies personalities into 16 types based on 4 preference dimensions
Energy Direction (E/I), Perception (S/N), Judgment (T/F), Lifestyle (J/P)

howTo.title: How to Take the Test
items: 48 questions total, 12 questions per dimension
Choose the answer that feels more natural to you
Don't overthink — answer based on your usual behavior
The test takes approximately 5-10 minutes

axes.title: 4 Preference Dimensions
items: E(Extraversion) vs I(Introversion): Where you get energy from
S(Sensing) vs N(Intuition): How you perceive information
T(Thinking) vs F(Feeling): How you make decisions
J(Judging) vs P(Perceiving): How you approach life

whatIs.title: What is the MBTI Personality Test?
whatIs.description: This 16-type personality test combines four preference pairs (E/I, S/N, T/F, J/P) from Carl Jung's psychological type theory to sort personalities into 16 types for self-reflection. It is an unofficial 48-question test made by ToolHub, not the official MBTI® assessment. MBTI and Myers-Briggs Type Indicator are registered trademarks of The Myers-Briggs Company; the official assessment is available through certified practitioners.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Questions appear one per screen. Pick one of five answers from "Strongly disagree" to "Strongly agree" and you move to the next question.
Use keys 1–5 to answer, and ← or Backspace to go back.
Your answers are saved in this tab, so a refresh will not lose your progress.
After all 48 questions you get your type and per-axis percentages. Share the result link and friends see the same result page.

tips.title: Pro Tips
items: Answer based on your usual self, not how you wish to be or what others expect of you.
If your E/I score is close to 50/50, you may be ambiverted—displaying traits of both types depending on context.
MBTI is not a fixed trait. Your type can shift with age, experience, and environment. Individual differences within the same type are also significant.
When using MBTI for career guidance, treat preferred types as suggestions—every type can excel in every profession.

items.q: Is this the official MBTI test?
items.a: No. MBTI® is a registered trademark of The Myers-Briggs Company, and the official assessment is a paid test given by certified practitioners. This unofficial test borrows the same four-preference concept, so do not use it for diagnosis, hiring, or career decisions.

items.q: Why does my result change each time I take the test?
items.a: Mood, recent experiences, and how you read the questions can all shift results. Axes marked Borderline (under 60%) flip most easily. Take the test on a few different days and look at which letters keep coming up.
In official MBTI samples from the US, INFJ is often cited as the rarest at roughly 1–2%, while ISFJ, ESFJ, and ISTJ are among the most common. Distributions vary considerably by country and sample.

items.q: Is MBTI appropriate as a hiring tool?
items.a: MBTI was not designed for selection. Its validity for predicting job performance is low, and professionals advise against using it in hiring decisions.
